Triggers.value: Night-time or waking up in the dark

Maladaptive Strategies.value: I drink alcohol, take medication or use drugs

vignette: Aleksander had always been a night owl, thriving in the quiet hours when the city was still. But that changed one fateful evening three years ago, when he witnessed a violent police crackdown on a peaceful protest while driving home from a late-night design meeting. As he watched in horror, officers in riot gear stormed into the crowd, beating protesters with batons and firing tear gas canisters into the air. His car was caught in the chaos, and Aleksander was forced to abandon it, fleeing on foot as police cars screeched to a halt around him. For weeks afterward, Aleksander struggled to shake off the memories of that night. He found himself waking up in the dark, his heart racing, with visions of baton-wielding officers looming over him. Even during the day, crowded places like train stations or shopping malls became unbearable - he'd push through throngs of people, anxiety clawing at his chest, as if the protesters' cries for help still echoed in his ears. As a graphic designer, Aleksander had always been skilled at creating order from chaos. But now, his designs seemed dull and lifeless to him, his creativity stifled by an unshakeable sense of unease. He began drinking more, using booze to numb the memories that haunted him. Medication and recreational drugs soon followed - anything to quiet the relentless fear-mongering voice in his head. Aleksander's loved ones grew increasingly concerned as he withdrew from social gatherings and stopped attending design events. His ex-wife, Sarah, tried to be supportive, but Aleksander couldn't bear the thought of being around her young daughter, whose bright smile reminded him of a protester he'd seen that night - a girl about the same age, with the same carefree laugh. At work, Aleksander found himself avoiding projects involving uniformed figures or law enforcement themes. His colleagues began to notice his growing unease, how he'd hastily excuse himself when discussions turned to politics or social justice. Even in meetings, if someone mentioned police brutality, Aleksander would instinctively cover his face with his hands - a nervous tic that left his coworkers puzzled. One evening, while driving home from work, Aleksander spotted a car similar to the one he'd been driving that fateful night. His heart skipped a beat as memories came flooding back: the screams, the sirens, the smell of smoke and sweat. Panic set in - he hastily pulled over, hands shaking as he rummaged for his phone. That moment marked a turning point for Aleksander. Realizing how far his anxiety had spiralled out of control, he knew he needed help. It wasn't just about avoiding triggers anymore; it was about rebuilding his life, rediscovering the creative spark that had once driven him. As he finally began to seek therapy, Aleksander couldn't shake off a lingering fear - would he ever be able to break free from the grip of those haunting memories and find peace in the darkness?
